title: For the sick and afraid
hook: the sound of a waiting room; Shantideva's list of wishes starts far away and comes close to home
tomorrow: what does an old poem wish someone stuck at the airport?

segments.voice: Yesterday Shantideva gave away the good of his whole poem: for all. Then he starts naming who all means, one by one.

Waiting rooms have their own sound. A TV nobody is watching. The hum of a vending machine. Somebody's knee bouncing, a phone buzzing, a name called that isn't yours. Shantideva's list of wishes passes through rooms like that, but it doesn't start there. It starts far off, in the hells of Buddhist teaching: may the cold find warmth, may the burning be cooled. Then the animals. Then, verse by verse, it comes closer, to the blind, the hungry, and then right into the waiting room: the sick, and the afraid.
screen: `A TV NOBODY IS WATCHING.` → `THE LIST STARTS FAR AWAY.` → `THEN IT COMES CLOSE TO HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the wish, in plain words. May the sick be freed from sickness. May the frightened stop being afraid. May the ones who are tied up go free, and the ones with no strength find some. And then the line closes on something quieter: may people think of helping one another. Notice what Shantideva can't do. A verse doesn't set a bone or shrink a fever, and the poem doesn't claim it does. So what's the wish for? Go back to chapter one of his guide. There he says there's wishing to go and actually going, like deciding on a trip and then walking the road. The wish comes first. It's how the bodhisattva's way begins. A wish said for a sick friend doesn't replace the casserole or the ride to the appointment. It's the thing that gets you to bring them. And the last line shows where the whole list has been heading. It isn't only that the sick get well. It's that people start looking out for each other. Say it slowly and listen to it: may they be well. Four words, and nobody is left out of they.
screen: `MAY THE SICK BE FREED.` · `MAY THE FRIGHTENED NOT FEAR.` · `FIRST THE WISH, THEN THE ROAD.` · `PEOPLE HELPING ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `MAY THEY BE WELL.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand open. For each of three people, press a fingertip to your thumb: someone who is sick, someone who is afraid, and someone you don't know at all. With each small press, say under your breath: may they be well. Then let the hand open and rest.
For the sick and afraid: Shantideva's verses wishing healing to the sick and an end to fear for the frightened.
screen: `FOR THE SICK AND AFRAID — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to this: may they be well, said even on the days you can't fix a thing. That's forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 1502 COUNTS.` → `SHANTIDEVA'S GUIDE · 47 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES AN OLD POEM WISH SOMEONE STUCK AT THE AIRPORT?`

howItsDone: Wishing well-being for others is part of daily practice in Buddhist communities; Mahayana practitioners recite dedication verses like Shantideva's, and loving-kindness wishes are said for the sick and the frightened by name.

match.prompt: the wishes, one by one — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: your grandpa is in the hospital three states away, and you can't visit until next month. what fits Shantideva's verses?
options: wish him well every day, and let the wish turn into calls and cards.
nothing until you can be there; a wish from far away is only words.
try not to think about it, since worrying won't heal him anyway.
fork.reveal: the verses don't claim to heal anyone. the wish comes first, like deciding on a trip, and it's what gets you on the road: the call, the card.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: fearlessness, freedom from fear. What the verse wishes for the frightened.

trapdoor: what you thought: a get-well card in verse.
what it means: Shantideva wishes healing to the sick and an end to fear for the frightened, knowing a verse can't do it alone; the wish turns the wisher toward helping.
what a scholar hears: chapter ten moves from the hells to human needs and ends with people thinking of one another's good, echoing chapter one's wish to go and actually going.
guess: wishing healing and an end to fear for others
a promise that a verse will make sick people well
a warning to stay away from anyone who is ill
recall: for all: the good handed on
two wings: seeing clearly, caring more

chat.says: ava's mom has surgery friday. routine, they say. ava's terrified and i can't fix anything.
options: Say the wish, even quietly: may she be well. Then just be there for Ava.
Tell her not to worry. Worrying won't change how the surgery goes.
Wishing does nothing if you can't fix it. Give her space till it's over.
chat.meaning: Shantideva wishes healing and freedom from fear even where he can't fix anything. The wish comes first, and it turns you toward helping.

Shantideva.meaning: the Buddhist monk and poet who wrote the Bodhicaryavatara

hells.meaning: in Buddhist teaching, realms of intense suffering, not eternal

bodhisattva.meaning: one who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 10.2–10.20 (wishes for beings in the hells, animals, the blind, the hungry; may the sick be freed, the frightened be fearless, the bound be freed, the weak gain strength, and people think of one another's good)
Bodhicaryavatara 1.15–1.16 (wishing to go and going: aspiring and engaged bodhicitta)
